fetched_contents.text: Water–gas shift reaction Reaction of carbon monoxide and water vapor The water–gas shift reaction (WGSR) describes the reaction of carbon monoxide and water vapor to form carbon dioxide and hydrogen: CO + H2O ⇌ CO2 + H2 The water gas shift reaction was discovered by Italian physicist Felice Fontana in 1780.[1][2] It was not until much later that the industrial value of this reaction was realized. Before the early 20th century, hydrogen was obtained by reacting steam under high pressure with iron to produce iron oxide and hydrogen. With the development of industrial processes that required hydrogen, such as the Haber–Bosch ammonia synthesis, a less expensive and more efficient method of hydrogen production was needed. As a resolution to this problem, the WGSR was combined with the gasification of coal to produce hydrogen. Applications The WGSR is a highly valuable industrial reaction that is used in the manufacture of ammonia, hydrocarbons, methanol, and hydrogen. Its most important application is in conjunction with the conversion of carbon monoxide from steam reforming of methane or other hydrocarbons in the production of hydrogen.[3] In the Fischer–Tropsch process, the WGSR is one of the most important reactions used to balance the H2/CO ratio. It provides a source of hydrogen at the expense of carbon monoxide, which is important for the production of high purity hydrogen for use in ammonia synthesis. The water–gas shift reaction may be an undesired side reaction in processes involving water and carbon monoxide, e.g. the rhodium-based Monsanto process. The iridium-based Cativa process uses less water, which suppresses this reaction. Fuel cells The WGSR can aid in the efficiency of fuel cells by increasing hydrogen production. The WGSR is considered a critical component in the reduction of carbon monoxide concentrations in cells that are susceptible to carbon monoxide poisoning such as the proton-exchange membrane (PEM) fuel cell.[4] The benefits of this application are two-fold: not only would the water gas shift reaction effectively reduce the concentration of carbon monoxide, but it would also increase the efficiency of the fuel cells by increasing hydrogen production.[4] Unfortunately, current commercial catalysts that are used in industrial water gas shift processes are not compatible with fuel cell applications.[5] With the high demand for clean fuel and the critical role of the water gas shift reaction in hydrogen fuel cells, the development of water gas shift catalysts for the application in fuel cell technology is an area of current research interest. Catalysts for fuel cell application would need to operate at low temperatures. Since the WGSR is slow at lower temperatures where equilibrium favors hydrogen production, WGS reactors require large amounts of catalysts, which increases their cost and size beyond practical application.[4] The commercial LTS catalyst used in large scale industrial plants is also pyrophoric in its inactive state and therefore presents safety concerns for consumer applications.[5] Developing a catalyst that can overcome these limitations is relevant to implementation of a hydrogen economy. Sorption enhanced water gas shift The WGS reaction is used in combination with the solid adsorption of CO2 in the sorption enhanced water gas shift (SEWGS) in order to produce a high pressure hydrogen stream from syngas.[6] Reaction conditions The equilibrium of this reaction shows a significant temperature dependence and the equilibrium constant decreases with an increase in temperature, that is, higher hydrogen formation is observed at lower temperatures. Temperature dependence With increasing temperature, the reaction rate increases, but hydrogen production becomes less favorable thermodynamically[7] since the water gas shift reaction is moderately exothermic; this shift in chemical equilibrium can be explained according to Le Chatelier's principle. Over the temperature range of 600–2000 K, the equilibrium constant for the WGSR has the following relationship:[5] K p = 10 − 2.4198 + 0.0003855 T + 2180.6 T {\displaystyle K_{\mathrm {p} }=10^{-2.4198+0.0003855T+{\frac {2180.6}{T}}}} In the range of 600-1200 K, the simpler expression derived by Moe[8] can be used: K p = e − 4.33 + 4577.8 T {\displaystyle K_{\mathrm {p} }=e^{-4.33+{\frac {4577.8}{T}}}} Alternatively, the equilibrium constant for the WGSR directly derived from thermodynamic quantities leads to:[9] l n ( K p ) = − 13.148 + 1.077 l n ( T ) + 5.44 10 − 4 T − 1.125 10 − 7 T 2 + 5693.5 T − 49170 T 2 {\displaystyle ln(K_{\mathrm {p} })=-13.148+1.077~~ln(T)+5.44~~10^{-4}~~T-1.125~~10^{-7}~~T^{2}+{\frac {5693.5}{T}}-{\frac {49170}{T^{2}}}} Practical concerns In order to take advantage of both the thermodynamics and kinetics of the reaction, the industrial scale water gas shift reaction is conducted in multiple adiabatic stages consisting of a high temperature shift (HTS) followed by a low temperature shift (LTS) with intersystem cooling.[10] The initial HTS takes advantage of the high reaction rates, but results in incomplete conversion of carbon monoxide. A subsequent low temperature shift reactor lowers the carbon monoxide content to <1%. Commercial HTS catalysts are based on iron oxide–chromium oxide and the LTS catalyst is a copper-based. The copper catalyst is susceptible to poisoning by sulfur. Sulfur compounds are removed prior to the LTS reactor by a guard bed. An important limitation for the HTS is the H2O/CO ratio where low ratios may lead to side reactions such as the formation of metallic iron, methanation, carbon deposition, and the Fischer–Tropsch reaction. fetched_contents.text: Catalysts in the water-gas shift reaction: A comparative review of industrial and academic contributions 1. Introduction Anthropogenic emissions of greenhouse gases such as; carbon dioxide (CO2), methane (CH4), nitrous oxides (NOx), and various halogenated compounds are a hazard to the environment, exacerbating global warming in recent years (Oyewole et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2011). The release of carbon dioxide, which is responsible for 80 % of the world's greenhouse gas emissions, proves to be the main driver of the greenhouse effect (Department for Energy Security and Net Zero, 2024; Ochedi et al., 2021; Rothenberg, 2023). Due to the substantial increase in energy consumption that has corresponded with global population growth and industrialization, the excessive carbon dioxide discharge is linked to the heavy reliance on fossil fuels, which accounts for more than 85 % of the world's energy demand (Oyewole et al., 2023). Given industrial units rely on non-renewable feedstocks to achieve higher efficiency, fossil fuel combustion facilities are the largest source of emissions; these facilities are primarily coal-based (Cui et al., 2011; Dutcher et al., 2011; He et al., 2012; Sharma and Ghoshal, 2015). In response to social and political pressures for decarbonisation, the industry has focused on carbon capture, utilisation, and storage (CCUS), which has the potential to reduce carbon dioxide intensity in the sector by 60 % (S. Cui et al., 2011; McLaughlin et al., 2023). On combustion, hydrogen only releases water (H2O) and emits no greenhouse gases, rendering it a reliable and efficient fuel alternative to fossil fuels (Doukas et al., 2018; Han and Shin, 2004; Midilli et al., 2005; Xie et al., 2013). Hydrogen has been found to be useful in fuel cells, rocket fuels, cooling agents, and oxygen removal due to its efficient combustibility and ease of pipeline transportation (Chen et al., 2010; Makaryan et al., 2022; Ramachandran, 1998; Turner, 2004). The increasing usage of hydrogen energy is facilitated by the constant development of novel concepts and innovations in Europe, Asia, and the USA (Makaryan et al., 2022). The most often utilised method for producing 95 % of hydrogen worldwide is steam methane reforming (SMR) (Brandon and Kurban, 2017). Using that approach, biomass, coal, or natural gas are reformed to generate hydrogen and carbon monoxide (Turner, 2004; V., 2007). Another growing alternative to hydrogen production is through the process of methanol steam reforming (Hu et al., 2024; R. Shu et al., 2024). Frequently, the water-gas shift (WGS) reaction proceeds to eliminate carbon monoxide (CO) while producing an increased amount of hydrogen (V., 2007). Owing to the WGS reaction's significance in producing hydrogen, the catalysis literature delves deeply into this process. The reversible, moderately exothermic process turns a mixture of carbon monoxide and water into hydrogen and carbon dioxide with the aid of a catalyst (Gogate, 2020; Newsome, 1980; Ratnasamy and Wagner, 2009). In addition, the WGS industry is continuously evolving to optimize the flowsheet to increase the hydrogen product yield and capture the CO2 by-product. Recently, there have been several studies exploring state of the art technologies such as sorption-enhanced WGS and membrane-based reactive separation to intensify WGS. These are processes that allow the separation and reaction steps to occur simultaneously (Margull et al., 2022, 2024). Industrially, the reversible reaction is implemented in stages to maximise the CO equilibrium conversion and avoid compromising reaction kinetics and selectivity (Zhu and Wachs, 2016). The first reactor, which is chemically kinetics driven, uses a high temperature water-gas shift (HT-WGS) reaction to produce an output CO concentration of 1 %–5 % (Mendes et al., 2010) over iron-oxide/chromium-based between a temperature ranging of 310 °C –450 °C (Rhodes and Hutchings, 2003; Zhu and Wachs, 2016) A low temperature water-gas (LT-WGS) reactor with a copper/zinc oxide catalyst is then placed in series and heated to a temperature of 200–250 °C (Zhu and Wachs, 2016). This is employed to get the outflow CO concentration down to less than 0.5 %, as thermodynamic equilibrium is the dominating mechanism (Mendes et al., 2010). While zinc and aluminium oxides are frequently added (Busca et al., 2024; Y. Chen et al., 2021; Rodriguez et al., 2019), further research has lately been done on the use of platinum and molybdenum in ceria-based catalysts (Moon, 2009) as well as gold and zirconia additions in LT-WGS (Carter et al., 2019) Transition metals, like iron, nickel, and copper, supported on a range of substrates, such as silica or alumina, are frequently used to aid in the conversion of carbon monoxide (Ratnasamy and Wagner, 2009) For WGS, there are numerous commercial catalysts available. ## How WGS is used in gas conditioning to increase H2/CO ratio

The water gas shift (WGS) reaction is used in gas conditioning to reduce carbon monoxide (CO) and increase hydrogen (H₂) concentration in a syngas stream, thereby raising the H₂/CO ratio. The basic chemistry is straightforward: carbon monoxide reacts with water vapor to form carbon dioxide and hydrogen, CO + H₂O ⇌ CO₂ + H₂ [N1-F1]. This means the feed entering WGS typically contains CO, water vapor, and possibly other syngas components, while the exit stream contains more H₂ and less CO, with CO₂ as a byproduct [N1-F1]. The shift reaction is reversible and moderately exothermic, and its equilibrium strongly favors lower temperatures because the equilibrium constant decreases with increasing temperature [N1-F1].

### What feed composition enters WGS and how it changes after shift
In industrial practice, WGS is often preceded by reforming or gasification steps that produce a CO-rich syngas, such as from steam methane reforming or coal gasification [N1-F1]. The feed composition therefore usually includes CO, H₂O, and sometimes other gases such as CO₂ or unreacted methane or hydrocarbons, depending on the upstream process [N1-F1]. After shift, the CO content is lowered, and the H₂ content is increased because the reaction consumes CO and H₂O while producing H₂ and CO₂ [N1-F1]. The shift is therefore a key conditioning step for adjusting the composition of the syngas stream before downstream processing [N1-F1].

### Why higher H₂/CO is needed for methanation
Higher H₂/CO is important because methanation reactions typically require a specific H₂/CO or H₂/CO₂ ratio to operate efficiently and selectively [N4-R4]. The Sabatier reaction, a common methanation pathway, produces methane from CO₂ and H₂ at elevated temperatures, and studies show that an H₂/CO₂ ratio close to 4, along with high pressure and moderate temperature, improves CO₂ conversion and selectivity [N4-R4]. Even for CO-based methanation, a favorable H₂/CO ratio is needed because the reaction consumes H₂ and CO to produce methane and water [N4-R3]. A higher H₂/CO ratio helps shift the reaction toward methane formation rather than side reactions or incomplete conversion, making methanation more efficient [N4-R4].

### How steam and temperature control the shift direction and selectivity
Steam and temperature are central to controlling the direction and selectivity of the WGS reaction. Steam addition increases the availability of water vapor, which shifts the equilibrium toward products by Le Chatelier’s principle and can improve conversion at lower temperatures [N3-R1]. Temperature has a dual effect: the reaction rate increases with temperature, but hydrogen production becomes less favorable thermodynamically because the equilibrium constant decreases with temperature [N1-F1]. This means that high-temperature shift reactors are kinetically favorable, while low-temperature shift reactors are thermodynamically favorable and better for maximizing CO conversion [N1-F1]. In industrial practice, this is usually managed with a two-stage configuration: a high-temperature shift reactor (HTS) followed by a low-temperature shift reactor (LTS) [N1-F1]. The first stage uses an iron-based catalyst and operates between 310 °C and 450 °C, while the second stage uses a copper-based catalyst and operates around 200 °C [N5-F3]. The overall result is a more selective and higher-conversion shift process that better prepares the gas for downstream methanation by increasing H₂ and lowering CO [N1-F1][N5-F3].

## Context for WGS integration with methanation and overall conditioning

### How WGS fits into the overall hydrogen production and conditioning sequence
WGS is typically integrated downstream of reforming or gasification steps in hydrogen production. In the conditioning sequence, the goal is to purify and adjust the syngas composition before it enters downstream processes such as methanation [N2-R3][N2-R4]. Steam methane reforming, for example, produces a hydrogen-rich gas stream that still contains CO and other impurities, so purification and conditioning are necessary to remove CO₂ and other contaminants [N2-R3][N2-R4]. WGS plays a central role in this sequence by reducing CO and increasing H₂, which is important for both hydrogen purity and for downstream methanation feed preparation [N1-F1][N2-R3].

### Tradeoffs between shift conversion, energy use, and downstream methanation
There are clear tradeoffs between shift conversion, energy use, and downstream methanation performance. High-temperature shift reactors can achieve faster kinetics and higher short-term conversion, but they are less thermodynamically favorable for CO removal [N1-F1]. Low-temperature shift reactors are more thermodynamically favorable and can push CO lower, but they require additional cooling and may reduce reaction rate [N1-F1]. Because methanation often requires a specific H₂/CO or H₂/CO₂ ratio, the choice of operating conditions must balance CO removal in WGS with the downstream methanation requirements [N4-R4]. Studies show that high-purity hydrogen production often uses a two-stage WGS configuration to maximize CO conversion while controlling methanol byproduct formation [N5-F3]. This means that, although higher shift conversion can reduce CO, it may also increase energy use and complicate downstream processing [N1-F1][N5-F3].

### Key operating conditions that balance H₂/CO ratio and process economics
Key operating conditions include temperature, pressure, steam-to-carbon ratio, and reactor staging. Lower temperatures favor thermodynamic conversion, but higher temperatures improve kinetics [N1-F1]. Steam addition is important because it shifts the equilibrium toward products and can improve selectivity and conversion [N3-R1]. Pressure also matters because the WGS equilibrium is pressure-dependent, and higher pressure can improve conversion of CO to CO₂ and H₂ [N1-F1]. In industrial practice, the WGS is often carried out in multiple adiabatic stages with cooling between stages, such as a high-temperature shift (HTS) followed by a low-temperature shift (LTS) [N1-F1]. This staging helps balance conversion, energy use, and downstream methanation requirements [N5-F3]. Overall, the best process economics come from selecting conditions that maximize H₂/CO ratio while keeping energy costs and reactor size within practical limits [N1-F1][N5-F3].

## CO₂-methanation requirements and why H₂/CO ratio matters for that pathway

### Methanation feed composition and the role of CO₂ in the reaction
Methanation feed composition is typically centered on CO or CO₂ plus H₂, depending on the pathway. The Sabatier process is a classic example in which CO₂ reacts with H₂ to produce methane and water [N4-R5][N6-R4]. In industrial methanation, feed composition is often designed to match the thermodynamic and kinetic requirements of the reaction [N4-R4]. A typical methanation feed may contain a mixture of CO and CO₂, along with excess H₂, because the reaction consumes both H₂ and CO or CO₂ to produce methane and water [N4-R3][N6-R4]. CO₂ is important because it is the carbon source in CO₂-based methanation, and its presence determines the stoichiometry of the reaction [N4-R5][N6-R4].

### Required H₂/CO or H₂/CO₂ ratio for efficient methanation
Efficient methanation requires a favorable H₂/CO or H₂/CO₂ ratio. One review explicitly states that an H₂/CO₂ ratio close to 4, high pressures (≥4 bar), and moderate temperatures ensure high CO₂ conversion and high selectivity for methane [N4-R4]. This aligns with the Sabatier reaction stoichiometry, where CO₂ + 4H₂ ⇌ CH₄ + 2H₂O and the reaction is exothermic [N6-R1][N6-R2]. The required ratio is not just a matter of stoichiometry; it also controls reaction direction and selectivity. If the H₂/CO or H₂/CO₂ ratio is too low, the reaction may become limited by CO or CO₂ availability and may favor side reactions or incomplete conversion [N4-R4][N6-R1]. In CO-based methanation, a similar balance is needed because the reaction also consumes H₂ and CO to produce methane and water [N4-R3]. A higher H₂/CO ratio improves conversion and selectivity by favoring methane formation over competing pathways [N4-R4].

### How WGS helps prepare the feed for methanation rather than directly producing methane
WGS helps prepare the feed for methanation by adjusting the syngas composition to meet the required H₂/CO or H₂/CO₂ ratio, rather than directly producing methane. The WGS reaction consumes CO and H₂O while producing H₂ and CO₂, effectively increasing the H₂ content and reducing CO content in the syngas [N1-F1]. This makes the resulting stream more compatible with methanation requirements [N1-F1][N4-R4]. In the context of methanation, WGS can be used to shift the feed from a CO-rich syngas toward a higher-H₂, lower-CO composition before entering methanation [N1-F1]. The WGS is therefore a conditioning step, not the final methane-producing step; it prepares the feed to optimize the methanation reaction [N1-F1][N4-R4]. This distinction is important because methanation is typically the downstream step that actually produces methane, while WGS is used to shape the feedstock for that reaction [N1-F1][N4-R4].

## What enhancements improve WGS performance and selectivity

### Which catalysts or catalyst supports improve shift activity and stability
WGS performance is strongly influenced by catalyst choice. The literature indicates that iron-oxide/chromium-based catalysts are commonly used for high-temperature shift (HTS), while copper/zinc oxide catalysts are used for low-temperature shift (LTS) [N1-F1][N5-F3]. Commercial catalysts include TOPSOE’s SK-501 Flex, Johnson Matthey’s KATALCO 71-series for HT-WGS, and Johnson Matthey’s KATALCO 83-series, TOPSOE’s LK-853 FENCE, and SHIFTMAX CLARIANT SERIES for LT-WGS [N3-F2]. These catalysts are tailored for different temperature regimes because the reaction is kinetically favorable at high temperatures and thermodynamically favorable at low temperatures [N1-F1]. Supports such as silica, alumina, and other oxides are also important because they stabilize the active metal and help manage side reactions [N3-F2]. Recent work highlights that global research is focused on improving conversion, stability, reducing poisoning, and minimizing side reactions, with studies exploring sulfur-resistant sour-gas shift and medium-temperature WGS [N3-F2].

### How pressure, temperature, and steam-to-carbon ratio affect reaction efficiency
Pressure, temperature, and steam-to-carbon ratio all affect WGS efficiency in different ways. Temperature has a dual effect: increasing temperature raises the reaction rate but reduces the thermodynamic favorability of hydrogen production because the equilibrium constant decreases with temperature [N1-F1]. Steam addition shifts the equilibrium toward products and can improve conversion and selectivity by Le Chatelier’s principle [N3-R1]. Pressure also matters because the WGS equilibrium is pressure-dependent; higher pressure can improve CO conversion and H₂ production [N1-F1]. The steam-to-carbon ratio is especially important because it influences the availability of water vapor and, therefore, the direction of the shift [N3-R1]. In industrial practice, the steam-to-carbon ratio is kept within a range that avoids side reactions such as methanation, carbon deposition, and Fischer–Tropsch-type reactions [N1-F1]. The optimal ratio depends on the process objective: higher steam can improve conversion, but excess steam may reduce CO conversion if the reaction becomes too far from equilibrium [N1-F1][N3-R1].

### Which engineering strategies maximize H₂/CO ratio while minimizing side reactions
Engineering strategies to maximize H₂/CO ratio while minimizing side reactions include staged reactor operation, temperature control, and membrane integration. A common industrial approach is to use a two-stage WGS configuration: a high-temperature shift reactor followed by a low-temperature shift reactor [N1-F1][N5-F3]. This staged approach allows the process to take advantage of both kinetics and thermodynamics, with the HTS improving short-term conversion and the LTS lowering CO to <1% [N1-F1]. Temperature control is critical because the reaction is strongly temperature-dependent, and operating at the right temperature can maximize CO conversion without excessive side reactions [N1-F1]. Membrane reactors are another advanced strategy; they can increase CO conversion and H₂ recovery by separating hydrogen from the reaction stream while maintaining CO in the recycle loop [N7-R1][N7-R4]. Pd-based and Pd-Ag membrane reactors are specifically noted for their ability to improve CO conversion and H₂ recovery in WGS [N7-R1][N7-R3]. These strategies collectively help maximize H₂/CO ratio while minimizing side reactions such as methanation, carbon deposition, and undesirable byproducts [N1-F1][N7-R4].
